fields.Front: Why must momentum be redefined as \(\gamma m\vec u\) in special relativity?
fields.Back: With \(m\vec u\), momentum is conserved in one inertial frame but not in another (the two-ball collision viewed from S′). \(\gamma m\vec u\) is conserved in every frame, as postulate 1 requires.
fields.SpeakFront: why must momentum be redefined as gamma m u in special relativity?
fields.SpeakBack: because m u is conserved in one inertial frame but not in another; gamma m u is conserved in every frame, as the first postulate requires
fields.Elaboration: Slides 5–6 set this up: the inelastic collision is fine in S and breaks in S′.

golden.note: Answers the red 'why?'. A why-card instead of a definition, because the definition is already carded.

fields.Front: Why can a constant force never accelerate a particle to \(c\)?
fields.Back: \(a=\dfrac{F}{m}\left(1-u^2/c^2\right)^{3/2}\to0\) as \(u\to c\): the same force produces less and less acceleration
fields.SpeakFront: why can a constant force never accelerate a particle to the speed of light?
fields.SpeakBack: because the acceleration equals F over m times one minus u squared over c squared, to the three halves, which goes to zero as u approaches c
fields.Elaboration: Equivalently, the force needed to keep accelerating diverges. That's why accelerators like the LHC approach c but never reach it.

golden.note: Answers the red 'we can't push to c?' with the formula as the reason. The formula alone is not its own card.

review.reason: this should be two cards, one being the formula, and one being the reasoning.
